name: Spirit Lake Tribe
land_summary: The Spirit Lake reservation was set aside by an 1867 treaty with the Sisseton and Wahpeton bands, on the south shore of Devils Lake in east-central North Dakota. Cut-Head Yanktonai families were placed there too. Allotment came soon after the Dawes Act of 1887, and by then non-Indian homesteaders had already claimed about 64,000 acres of reservation land. In 1904 Congress ratified a sale of the unallotted land, and a proclamation signed by T.R. opened about 88,000 acres to settlers through a lottery. Today most land inside the roughly 245,000-acre boundary is privately owned fee land, with tribal and allotted trust land scattered among it. In 2025 the Tribe regained 680 acres that the Bureau of Indian Affairs had handed to the Fish and Wildlife Service in 1959 to grow hay for the bison at the nearby game preserve.

timeline.event: A treaty with the Sisseton and Wahpeton bands sets aside the reservation at Devils Lake.
Congress ratifies an amended agreement to sell the unallotted land, and a proclamation signed by T.R. opens about 88,000 acres to settlement.
The Bureau of Indian Affairs transfers 680 acres to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to grow hay for bison at the nearby game preserve.
The 680 acres return to trust for the Spirit Lake Nation.

notes: The opened acreage conflicts: the 1904 proclamation says about 88,000 acres, and ND Studies says 100,000. The summary uses the proclamation figure. The Tribe's acreage table is from 1998, and its four categories add up to 6 acres less than its stated total of 245,141. ND Studies says the Dakota held just over 50,000 acres when allotment ended in 1934. That is single-source, so it was left out. Tribal Business News reports the Tribe is seeking about 300 more acres of federal game-preserve land. The 1904 proclamation reserved land for Sullys Hill Park, the earlier name of what is now White Horse Hill. A reviewer should decide whether to mention that link.
